claim: Ruijs-Aalfs syndrome is a segmental progeroid syndrome resulting from mutations in the SPRTN gene.
source: Ruijs-Aalfs syndrome is a segmental progeroid syndrome resulting from mutations in the SPRTN gene.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about the syndrome.

claim: Cells derived from patients with SPRTN mutations elicit genomic instability.
source: Cells derived from patients with SPRTN mutations elicit genomic instability and people afflicted with this syndrome developed hepatocellular carcinoma.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: People afflicted with Ruijs-Aalfs syndrome developed hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: Cells derived from patients with SPRTN mutations elicit genomic instability and people afflicted with this syndrome developed hepatocellular carcinoma.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and referenced in the introduction.

claim: SPRTN is a DNA-dependent mammalian protease.
source: We show that SPRTN is a DNA-dependent mammalian protease required for resolving cytotoxic DNA-protein crosslinks (DPCs)— a function that had only been attributed to the metalloprotease Wss1 in budding yeast.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through in vitro protease assays showing DNA-dependent activity.

claim: SPRTN is required for resolving cytotoxic DNA-protein crosslinks (DPCs).
source: We show that SPRTN is a DNA-dependent mammalian protease required for resolving cytotoxic DNA-protein crosslinks (DPCs)— a function that had only been attributed to the metalloprotease Wss1 in budding yeast.
evidence: This is demonstrated through ICE assays showing DPC accumulation in SPRTN-deficient cells.

claim: DPC resolution function had only been attributed to the metalloprotease Wss1 in budding yeast prior to this study.
source: We show that SPRTN is a DNA-dependent mammalian protease required for resolving cytotoxic DNA-protein crosslinks (DPCs)— a function that had only been attributed to the metalloprotease Wss1 in budding yeast.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: SPRTN and Wss1 function distinctly in vivo to resolve DPCs.
source: We provide genetic evidence that SPRTN and Wss1 function distinctly in vivo to resolve DPCs.
evidence: This is demonstrated through yeast complementation experiments showing SPRTN cannot functionally replace Wss1.

claim: Upon DNA and ubiquitin binding, SPRTN can elicit proteolytic activity.
source: Upon DNA and ubiquitin binding, SPRTN can elicit proteolytic activity; cleaving DPC substrates and itself.
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vitro protease assays showing enhanced activity with DNA and ubiquitin.

claim: SPRTN cleaves DPC substrates and itself.
source: Upon DNA and ubiquitin binding, SPRTN can elicit proteolytic activity; cleaving DPC substrates and itself.
evidence: This is shown through Western blot analysis of SPRTN cleavage products and substrate cleavage assays.

claim: SPRTN null cells are impaired in the resolution of covalent DPCs in vivo.
source: SPRTN null cells or cells derived from patients with Ruijs-Aalfs syndrome are impaired in the resolution of covalent DPCs in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated through ICE assays showing persistent Top2 DPCs in SPRTN-KO cells.

claim: Cells derived from patients with Ruijs-Aalfs syndrome are impaired in the resolution of covalent DPCs in vivo.
source: SPRTN null cells or cells derived from patients with Ruijs-Aalfs syndrome are impaired in the resolution of covalent DPCs in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated through ICE assays and γ-H2AX staining in patient-derived cells.

claim: SPRTN is a mammalian protease required for resolving DNA-protein crosslinks in vivo.
source: Collectively, SPRTN is a mammalian protease required for resolving DNA-protein crosslinks in vivo whose function is compromised in Ruijs-Aalfs syndrome patients.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by multiple experimental approaches including ICE assays and clonogenic survival assays.

claim: SPRTN function is compromised in Ruijs-Aalfs syndrome patients.
source: Collectively, SPRTN is a mammalian protease required for resolving DNA-protein crosslinks in vivo whose function is compromised in Ruijs-Aalfs syndrome patients.
evidence: This is demonstrated through functional assays showing impaired DPC resolution in patient cells.

claim: DNA is continuously subjected to various forms of damage stemming from endogenous and exogenous sources.
source: DNA is continuously subjected to various forms of damage stemming from endogenous and exogenous sources.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction.

claim: DNA lesions can include UV-induced photoproducts, inter- and intra-strand crosslinks, abasic sites, oxidative damage, bulky chemical lesions or single and double strand breaks.
source: The DNA lesions are highly diverse and can include UV-induced photoproducts, inter- and intra-strand crosslinks, abasic sites, oxidative damage, bulky chemical lesions or single and double strand breaks (Hoeijmakers, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Specialized DNA repair systems have evolved to repair the multitude of lesions.
source: Specialized DNA repair systems have evolved to repair the multitude of lesions and these repair systems collectively contribute to maintaining genome stability and cellular survival (Jackson and Bartek, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: DNA repair systems collectively contribute to maintaining genome stability and cellular survival.
source: Specialized DNA repair systems have evolved to repair the multitude of lesions and these repair systems collectively contribute to maintaining genome stability and cellular survival (Jackson and Bartek, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Naturally occurring cellular processes, such as histone demethylation, can lead to covalent DNA-protein crosslinks (DPCs) of neighboring proteins.
source: Naturally occurring cellular processes, such as histone demethylation, can also lead to covalent DNA-protein crosslinks (DPCs) of neighboring proteins (Shi et al., 2004; Tsukada et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DPCs, if not resolved, are formidable impediments to ongoing DNA replication forks and gene transcription.
source: DPCs, if not resolved, are formidable impediments to ongoing DNA replication forks, gene transcription (Stingele and Jentsch, 2015) and conceivably chromatin remodeling.
evidence: This is supported by citation and logical inference.

claim: DPCs can conceivably impede chromatin remodeling.
source: DPCs, if not resolved, are formidable impediments to ongoing DNA replication forks, gene transcription (Stingele and Jentsch, 2015) and conceivably chromatin remodeling.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the nature of DPCs.

claim: DNA replication machinery creates DNA supercoiling ahead of and behind the replication fork.
source: As DNA replication machinery synthesizes new DNA at the replication fork, DNA supercoiling is created ahead of and behind the replication fork, profoundly altering DNA topology.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA replication.

claim: Topoisomerases 1 and 2 relax DNA supercoiling by breaking and re-ligating one or both strands of the DNA, respectively.
source: Topoisomerases 1 and 2 (Top1 and Top2) relax DNA supercoiling by breaking and re-ligating one or both strands of the DNA, respectively (Pommier and Marchand, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Top1 and Top2 naturally form DPCs as part of an obligate intermediate step required for the re-ligation step.
source: Top1 and Top2 naturally form DPCs as part of an obligate intermediate step required for the re-ligation step.
evidence: This is established knowledge about topoisomerase mechanism.

claim: Malfunction in the re-ligation steps cause Top1 and Top2 to be permanently trapped on DNA in the form of DPCs.
source: Because enzymatic reactions have an intrinsic error rate, malfunction in the re-ligation steps cause Top1 and Top2 to be permanently trapped on DNA in the form of DPCs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about topoisomerase errors.

claim: Wss1 was shown to counteract DPCs induced by Camptothecin (CPT) or formaldehyde.
source: Wss1 was shown to counteract DPCs induced by the anti-cancer agent Camptothecin (CPT) or those induced by the unspecific crosslinking agent, formaldehyde.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Yeast cells missing key components of the DPC repair system succumb to cell death upon exposure to CPT.
source: Moreover, yeast cells missing key components of the DPC repair system succumb to cell death upon exposure to CPT, underscoring the importance of DPC removal.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: An analogous DPC repair mechanism has been identified in vitro in Xenopus laevis egg extract.
source: In Xenopus laevis egg extract, an analogous DPC repair mechanism has been identified in vitro (Duxin et al., 2014), however the identity of the protease(s) involved was not elucidated.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The identity of the protease(s) involved in DPC repair in Xenopus laevis egg extract was not elucidated.
source: In Xenopus laevis egg extract, an analogous DPC repair mechanism has been identified in vitro (Duxin et al., 2014), however the identity of the protease(s) involved was not elucidated.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge based on cited work.

claim: It is unknown whether a protease that counteracts DPCs exists in mammalian cells.
source: However, it is unknown whether a protease that counteracts DPCs exists in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is stated as the knowledge gap this study addresses.

claim: SPRTN was initially discovered as being an important protein for translesion DNA synthesis.
source: SPRTN (also known as Dvc1 or C1orf124) was initially discovered as being an important protein for translesion DNA synthesis (Centore et al., 2012; Davis et al., 2012; Ghosal et al., 2012; Juhasz et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013; Machida et al., 2012; Mosbech et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: SPRTN is a multi-domain containing protein that is endowed with an SprT-like domain, a SHP and PIP box as well as a ubiquitin binding zinc finger (UBZ) domain.
source: SPRTN is a multi-domain containing protein that is endowed with an SprT-like domain, a SHP and PIP box as well as a ubiquitin binding zinc finger (UBZ) domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SPRTN structure.

claim: SPRTN binding to ubiquitin and to PCNA was suggested to be critical for its recruitment to sites of UV-induced DNA damage.
source: SPRTN binding to ubiquitin and to PCNA was suggested to be critical for its recruitment to sites of UV-induced DNA damage, while interactions with a ubiquitin-dependent molecular segregase p97 (known as VCP in higher eukaryotes and Cdc48 in yeast) are implicated in extraction of the translesion polymerase Pol eta (Davis et al., 2012; Mosbech et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Interactions between SPRTN and p97 are implicated in extraction of the translesion polymerase Pol eta.
source: SPRTN binding to ubiquitin and to PCNA was suggested to be critical for its recruitment to sites of UV-induced DNA damage, while interactions with a ubiquitin-dependent molecular segregase p97 (known as VCP in higher eukaryotes and Cdc48 in yeast) are implicated in extraction of the translesion polymerase Pol eta (Davis et al., 2012; Mosbech et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It was proposed that SPRTN and Wss1 could belong to a related family of DPC-resolving proteases based on the presence of an SprT-like metalloprotease domain with similarity to the WLM domain in Wss1.
source: Based on the presence of an SprT-like metalloprotease domain with similarity to the WLM domain in Wss1, it was proposed that SPRTN and Wss1 could belong to a related family of DPC-resolving proteases (Stingele et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: SPRTN is an essential protein, as mice with homozygous null alleles die very early during embryonic development.
source: Later work revealed that SPRTN is an essential protein, as mice with homozygous null alleles die very early during embryonic development (Maskey et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Hypomorphic murine SPRTN alleles render mice with premature aging phenotypes.
source: Furthermore, hypomorphic murine SPRTN alleles render mice with premature aging phenotypes (Maskey et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Rare SPRTN germ-line mutations were identified in three patients from two unrelated families afflicted with Ruijs-Aalfs syndrome.
source: Very recently, we identified rare SPRTN germ-line mutations in three patients from two unrelated families afflicted with Ruijs-Aalfs syndrome (Lessel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The first proband inherited homozygous point mutations that resulted in a premature stop codon and subsequent loss of the carboxyl-terminal half of the SPRTN protein.
source: The first proband inherited homozygous point mutations that resulted in a premature stop codon and subsequent loss of the carboxyl-terminal half of the SPRTN protein (herein referred to as SPRTN-∆C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The second set of probands inherited biallelic mutations such that one allele was a point mutation similar to SPRTN-∆C, while the second allele has a tyrosine to cysteine substitution at position 117.
source: The second set of probands inherited biallelic mutations such that one allele was also a point mutation that, coincidentally, is highly reminiscent to the SPRTN-∆C, while the second allele has a tyrosine to cysteine substitution at position 117 (herein referred to as SPRTN-Y117C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Individuals harboring SPRTN mutations were shown to have segmental progeroid features and developed early onset hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: Individuals harboring these mutations were shown to have segmental progeroid features and developed early onset hepatocellular carcinoma (Lessel et al., 2014; Ruijs et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cells derived from affected individuals showed genomic instability associated with DNA replication stress.
source: In addition, cells derived from affected individuals showed genomic instability associated with DNA replication stress.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: DNA fiber assays confirmed slower replication fork movements in cells from affected individuals.
source: DNA fiber assays confirmed slower replication fork movements in cells from affected individuals and the slowing of replication forks was further exacerbated with the replication inhibitor Aphidicolin (Lessel et al., 2014), suggesting that cells with SPRTN mutations had difficulty replicating through blocking lesions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The slowing of replication forks was further exacerbated with the replication inhibitor Aphidicolin in cells from affected individuals.
source: DNA fiber assays confirmed slower replication fork movements in cells from affected individuals and the slowing of replication forks was further exacerbated with the replication inhibitor Aphidicolin (Lessel et al., 2014), suggesting that cells with SPRTN mutations had difficulty replicating through blocking lesions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Cells with SPRTN mutations had difficulty replicating through blocking lesions.
source: DNA fiber assays confirmed slower replication fork movements in cells from affected individuals and the slowing of replication forks was further exacerbated with the replication inhibitor Aphidicolin (Lessel et al., 2014), suggesting that cells with SPRTN mutations had difficulty replicating through blocking lesions.
evidence: This is inferred from the DNA fiber assay results.

claim: SPRTN and Wss1 share some common domains like a zinc metalloprotease domain and a SHP/VIM domain.
source: Although SPRTN and Wss1 share some common domains like a zinc metalloprotease domain and a SHP/VIM domain (p97/Cdc48 binding), they are also distinct in that they recognize substrates differently.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and supported by citations.

claim: SPRTN and Wss1 are distinct in that they recognize substrates differently.
source: Although SPRTN and Wss1 share some common domains like a zinc metalloprotease domain and a SHP/VIM domain (p97/Cdc48 binding), they are also distinct in that they recognize substrates differently.
evidence: This is supported by the description of their different binding domains.

claim: SPRTN preferentially binds to ubiquitin via its UBZ domain.
source: SPRTN preferentially binds to ubiquitin via its UBZ domain whereas Wss1 binds to SUMO via its SIM motives (Figure 1A) (Balakirev et al., 2015; Centore et al., 2012; Davis et al., 2012; Ghosal et al., 2012; Juhasz et al., 2012; Machida et al., 2012; Mosbech et al., 2012; Stingele et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Wss1 binds to SUMO via its SIM motives.
source: SPRTN preferentially binds to ubiquitin via its UBZ domain whereas Wss1 binds to SUMO via its SIM motives (Figure 1A) (Balakirev et al., 2015; Centore et al., 2012; Davis et al., 2012; Ghosal et al., 2012; Juhasz et al., 2012; Machida et al., 2012; Mosbech et al., 2012; Stingele et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The overall amino acid sequence conservation between SPRTN and Wss1 is relatively poor, particularly within the protease domains.
source: Despite the similarities in domain organization, the overall amino acid sequence conservation between SPRTN and Wss1 is relatively poor, particularly within the protease domains (Figure 1B), sharing only the conserved signature HEXXH motif found in the SprT family of metalloproteases, with glutamic acid being the catalytic amino acid.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B through sequence alignment.

claim: SPRTN and Wss1 share only the conserved signature HEXXH motif found in the SprT family of metalloproteases, with glutamic acid being the catalytic amino acid.
source: Despite the similarities in domain organization, the overall amino acid sequence conservation between SPRTN and Wss1 is relatively poor, particularly within the protease domains (Figure 1B), sharing only the conserved signature HEXXH motif found in the SprT family of metalloproteases, with glutamic acid being the catalytic amino acid.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and is established knowledge about metalloprotease catalytic motifs.

claim: Wss1 provides resistance to CPT in the absence of Tdp1.
source: Recently, it was shown that Wss1 provides resistance to CPT in the absence of Tdp1, a tyrosyl phosphodiesterase that removes Top1 remnants from 3' ends of DNA (Liu et al., 2002; Pommier et al., 2014; Pouliot et al., 1999), such that Wss1 and Tdp1 double deletion mutant strains die upon exposure to the DPC-inducing drug CPT (Balakirev et al., 2015; Stingele et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tdp1 is a tyrosyl phosphodiesterase that removes Top1 remnants from 3' ends of DNA.
source: Recently, it was shown that Wss1 provides resistance to CPT in the absence of Tdp1, a tyrosyl phosphodiesterase that removes Top1 remnants from 3' ends of DNA (Liu et al., 2002; Pommier et al., 2014; Pouliot et al., 1999), such that Wss1 and Tdp1 double deletion mutant strains die upon exposure to the DPC-inducing drug CPT (Balakirev et al., 2015; Stingele et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Wss1 and Tdp1 double deletion mutant strains die upon exposure to CPT.
source: Recently, it was shown that Wss1 provides resistance to CPT in the absence of Tdp1, a tyrosyl phosphodiesterase that removes Top1 remnants from 3' ends of DNA (Liu et al., 2002; Pommier et al., 2014; Pouliot et al., 1999), such that Wss1 and Tdp1 double deletion mutant strains die upon exposure to the DPC-inducing drug CPT (Balakirev et al., 2015; Stingele et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: wss1∆ tdp1∆ cells accumulate spontaneous second-site mutations that often suppressed the CPT-induced lethality.
source: It is noteworthy that wss1∆ tdp1∆ cells accumulate spontaneous second-site mutations that often suppressed the CPT-induced lethality.
evidence: This is stated as an observation that motivated the experimental design.

claim: Wss1 depletion occurred as rapidly as 40 min after doxycycline treatment using the dual protein depletion system.
source: Using this system, Wss1 depletion occurred as rapidly as 40 min after doxycycline treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and without overt consequences to the overall fitness of the cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing Western blot time course.

claim: Wss1 depletion occurred without overt consequences to the overall fitness of the cells.
source: Using this system, Wss1 depletion occurred as rapidly as 40 min after doxycycline treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and without overt consequences to the overall fitness of the cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system.

claim: wss1∆ tdp1∆ cells lost viability when exposed to CPT.
source: Consistent with previous reports, wss1∆ tdp1∆ cells lost viability when exposed to CPT (Mullally et al., 2015; Stingele et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Expression of SPRTN could not support the growth of wss1∆ tdp1∆ cells on CPT containing media.
source: Surprisingly, expression of SPRTN could not support the growth of wss1∆ tdp1∆ cells on CPT containing media (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C through yeast spot assay.

claim: SPRTN failed to complement Wss1 activity when SPRTN protein levels was increased to high levels using the inducible Galactose promoter.
source: SPRTN also failed to complement Wss1 activity when SPRTN protein levels was increased to high levels using the inducible Galactose promoter (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: SPRTN expression is readily detected by Western blot analysis in yeast.
source: The lack of functional complementation was not simply due to poor induction of SPRTN expression or a failure of SPRTN to reach the nucleus, as SPRTN expression is readily detected by Western blot analysis and its expression co-localizes with DAPI nuclear stain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: SPRTN expression co-localizes with DAPI nuclear stain in yeast.
source: The lack of functional complementation was not simply due to poor induction of SPRTN expression or a failure of SPRTN to reach the nucleus, as SPRTN expression is readily detected by Western blot analysis and its expression co-localizes with DAPI nuclear stain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ectopic SPRTN expression induced a slow-growth phenotype in a catalytic-dependent manner in yeast.
source: We did observe, however, that ectopic SPRTN expression induced a slow-growth phenotype, in a catalytic-dependent manner, such that neither SPRTN-E112A nor SPRTN-Y117C expression induced this slow-growth phenotype in tdp1∆ cells.
evidence: This is observed in the yeast spot assay experiments.

claim: Neither SPRTN-E112A nor SPRTN-Y117C expression induced a slow-growth phenotype in tdp1∆ cells.
source: We did observe, however, that ectopic SPRTN expression induced a slow-growth phenotype, in a catalytic-dependent manner, such that neither SPRTN-E112A nor SPRTN-Y117C expression induced this slow-growth phenotype in tdp1∆ cells.
evidence: This is observed in the yeast spot assay experiments.

claim: SPRTN-E112A and SPRTN-Y117C are catalytically inactive in yeast.
source: This genetic assay suggests that SPRTN-E112A and SPRTN-Y117C are catalytically inactive in yeast and that SPRTN expression elicits a dominant negative function over endogenous Wss1.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of slow-growth phenotype.

claim: SPRTN expression elicits a dominant negative function over endogenous Wss1 in yeast.
source: This genetic assay suggests that SPRTN-E112A and SPRTN-Y117C are catalytically inactive in yeast and that SPRTN expression elicits a dominant negative function over endogenous Wss1.
evidence: This is inferred from the slow-growth phenotype observed with SPRTN expression.

claim: SPRTN cannot functionally complement Wss1 function due to either additional regulation of SPRTN not present in yeast or to inherently different pathways between yeast and metazoan cells involved in DPC resolution.
source: Taken together, we conclude that SPRTN cannot functionally complement Wss1 function due to either additional regulation of SPRTN not present in yeast or to inherently different pathways between yeast and metazoan cells involved in DPC resolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the complementation experiments.

claim: SPRTN-KO cells were more sensitive to formaldehyde, CPT, and Etoposide treatments than control MEFs.
source: We found that SPRTN-KO cells were more sensitive to formaldehyde, CPT, and Etoposide treatments than control MEFs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A through clonogenic survival assays.

claim: Top2 DPCs were not appreciably detected in untreated cells.
source: Using this experimental approach, Top2 DPCs were not appreciably detected in untreated cells but were detected in DNA isolated from control SPRTN cells treated with Etoposide for 0.5 hr (Figure 2C), which is consistent with previous reports (Subramanian et al., 1995).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C through ICE assay.

claim: Top2 DPCs were detected in DNA isolated from control SPRTN cells treated with Etoposide for 0.5 hr.
source: Using this experimental approach, Top2 DPCs were not appreciably detected in untreated cells but were detected in DNA isolated from control SPRTN cells treated with Etoposide for 0.5 hr (Figure 2C), which is consistent with previous reports (Subramanian et al., 1995).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C through ICE assay and is consistent with previous reports.

claim: The Top2 signal diminished 1 hr after Etoposide treatment in control SPRTN cells, indicating that Top2 had been cleared from DNA.
source: The Top2 signal diminished 1 hr after Etoposide treatment, indicating that Top2 had been cleared from DNA.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C through ICE assay.

claim: In SPRTN-KO MEFs, Top2 signals are sustained throughout the duration of the time course.
source: In contrast to control MEFs, Top2 signals are sustained throughout the duration of the time course in SPRTN-KO MEFs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C through ICE assay.

claim: Top2 is not proteolyzed in cells lacking the SPRTN protease.
source: These results indicate that Top2 is not proteolyzed in cells lacking the SPRTN protease.
evidence: This is inferred from the sustained Top2 signal in SPRTN-KO cells.

claim: Knockout MEFs reconstituted with SPRTN-WT are able to resolve Top2cc from DNA, albeit with slower kinetics than the control SPRTN MEFs probably due to low levels of ectopic SPRTN expression.
source: As expected, knockout MEFs reconstituted with SPRTN-WT are able to resolve Top2cc from DNA, albeit with slower kinetics than the control SPRTN MEFs probably due to low levels of ectopic SPRTN expression.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and the slower kinetics is attributed to expression levels.

claim: SPRTN-KO MEFs reconstituted with SPRTN-∆C were delayed in Top2cc resolution.
source: Contrary to SPRTN-WT, SPRTN-KO MEFs reconstituted with SPRTN-∆C were delayed in Top2cc resolution under these conditions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C through ICE assay.

claim: SPRTN-KO MEFs could not be stably reconstituted with either SPRTN-E112A or SPRTN-Y117C.
source: Notably, SPRTN-KO MEFs could not be stably reconstituted with either SPRTN-E112A or SPRTN-Y117C.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the reconstitution experiments.

claim: SPRTN-KO MEFs reconstituted with either SPRTN-E112A or SPRTN-Y117C by transient transfection, failed to resolve Top2 DPCs.
source: Nevertheless, SPRTN-KO MEFs reconstituted with either SPRTN-E112A or SPRTN-Y117C by transient transfection, failed to resolve Top2 DPCs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C through ICE assay.

claim: SPRTN-E112A and SPRTN-Y117C alleles code for mutant SPRTN proteins lacking essential proteolytic activity.
source: This finding is consistent with the notion that these alleles code for mutant SPRTN proteins lacking essential proteolytic activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the failure to resolve Top2 DPCs.

claim: SPRTN is the mammalian protease responsible for DPC removal.
source: These results strongly suggest that SPRTN is the mammalian protease responsible for DPC removal and that this function is compromised in cells expressing SPRTN-Y117C, SPRTN-E112A or SPRTN-∆C mutant proteins.
evidence: This is concluded from the ICE assay results showing DPC accumulation in SPRTN-deficient cells.

claim: DPC removal function is compromised in cells expressing SPRTN-Y117C, SPRTN-E112A or SPRTN-∆C mutant proteins.
source: These results strongly suggest that SPRTN is the mammalian protease responsible for DPC removal and that this function is compromised in cells expressing SPRTN-Y117C, SPRTN-E112A or SPRTN-∆C mutant proteins.
evidence: This is shown through ICE assays with mutant proteins.

claim: SPRTN contains an SprT-like domain within its amino-terminus with the characteristic HEXXH catalytic signature motif found in zinc-dependent metalloproteases.
source: SPRTN contains an SprT-like domain within its amino-terminus with the characteristic HEXXH catalytic signature motif found in zinc-dependent metalloproteases (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and is established knowledge about metalloprotease motifs.

claim: Specific SPRTN cleavage fragments can be detected by Western blot analysis or live-cell imaging when SPRTN is over-expressed in cells.
source: Consistent with SPRTN being a protease, specific SPRTN cleavage fragments can be detected by Western blot analysis or live-cell imaging when SPRTN is over-expressed in cells (Figure 3A and B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3A, 3B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: SPRTN fragments are not detected when the catalytic glutamic acid in the HEXXH catalytic motif is mutated to alanine (E112A).
source: Importantly, the SPRTN fragments are not detected when the catalytic glutamic acid in the HEXXH catalytic motif is mutated to alanine (E112A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A similar attenuation of proteolytic fragments is observed when cells express the SPRTN-Y117C or SPRTN-∆C.
source: Interestingly, a similar attenuation of proteolytic fragments is observed when cells express the SPRTN-Y117C or SPRTN-∆C (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Histones were significantly over-represented as candidate SPRTN substrates in an unbiased protease screen using mass spectrometry.
source: In this screen we found that histones were significantly over-represented as candidate SPRTN substrates.
evidence: This is from a mass spectrometry screen for SPRTN substrates.

claim: Core histones can be relevant SPRTN substrates as they are intimately associated with DNA and are poised to become crosslinked upon exposure to endogenous formaldehyde.
source: It is likely that core histones can be relevant SPRTN substrates as they are intimately associated with DNA and are poised to become crosslinked upon exposure to endogenous formaldehyde.
evidence: This is logical inference based on histone-DNA association.

claim: A clear histone H3 fragment can be observed when SPRTN is overexpressed in 293T-HEK cells.
source: Consistent with this initial finding, we can observe the presence of a clear histone H3 fragment when SPRTN is overexpressed in 293T-HEK cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B through Western blot.

claim: The histone H3 cleavage product is not detected when SPRTN-E112A is over-expressed irrespective of stimulation with Etoposide and despite its chromatin recruitment.
source: Importantly, the histone H3 cleavage product is not detected when SPRTN-E112A is over-expressed irrespective of stimulation with Etoposide and despite its chromatin recruitment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), consistent with this mutation being catalytically inactive.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: SPRTN-∆C overexpression does not produce histone H3 cleavage fragments despite the fact that SPRTN-∆C is recruited to chromatin.
source: We next assessed the effect of SPRTN-∆C overexpression with respect to histone H3 cleavage. Notably, SPRTN-∆C overexpression does not produce histone H3 cleavage fragments despite the fact that we observe SPRTN-∆C chromatin recruitment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: SPRTN needs the C-terminus region to either target histone H3 or for DNA binding.
source: This result suggests that SPRTN needs the C-terminus region to either target histone H3 or for DNA binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of histone H3 cleavage by SPRTN-∆C.

claim: SPRTN can directly bind to DNA.
source: To distinguish between these two possibilities, we asked if SPRTN could directly bind to DNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated through EMSA experiments shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: As SPRTN levels were gradually increased, a corresponding increase in the electrophoretic mobility of the DNA probe was observed, indicative of SPRTN binding to single or double stranded DNA.
source: As SPRTN levels were gradually increased, we observed a corresponding increase in the electrophoretic mobility of the DNA probe, indicative of SPRTN binding to single or double stranded DNA (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and D through EMSA.

claim: The electrophoretic mobility shift is not detected when SPRTN-∆C1–216 protein is employed in the EMSA assay.
source: The electrophoretic mobility shift is not detected when we employ the SPRTN-∆C1–216 protein in this EMSA assay.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and D through EMSA.

claim: A region(s) located in the carboxyl-terminal half of SPRTN contains a DNA binding domain as detected in purified in vitro binding assays.
source: This result suggests that a region(s) located in the carboxyl-terminal half of SPRTN contains a DNA binding domain as detected in purified in vitro binding assays and that this domain is probably required to target histone H3 for degradation in cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the EMSA results showing loss of DNA binding in SPRTN-∆C.

claim: The DNA binding domain in the carboxyl-terminal half of SPRTN is probably required to target histone H3 for degradation in cells.
source: This result suggests that a region(s) located in the carboxyl-terminal half of SPRTN contains a DNA binding domain as detected in purified in vitro binding assays and that this domain is probably required to target histone H3 for degradation in cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined EMSA and histone cleavage results.

claim: Purified SPRTN elicits auto-cleaving activity in the presence of double stranded DNA similar to that observed in vivo.
source: Purified SPRTN elicits auto-cleaving activity in the presence of double stranded DNA similar to that observed in vivo (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A through in vitro cleavage assays.

claim: The auto-cleaving activity is dependent on the conserved catalytic glutamic acid residue at position 112, because the SPRTN-E112A mutant is devoid of autocatalytic activity.
source: Importantly, the auto-cleaving activity is dependent on the conserved catalytic glutamic acid residue at position 112, because the SPRTN-E112A mutant is devoid of autocatalytic activity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A through in vitro cleavage assays.

claim: SPRTN autocatalytic activity is inhibited by the zinc chelator, 1,10-Phenantroline, indicating that SPRTN is a zinc-dependent metalloprotease.
source: In addition, SPRTN autocatalytic activity is inhibited by the zinc chelator, 1,10-Phenantroline, indicating that SPRTN is a zinc-dependent metalloprotease.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A through in vitro cleavage assays with inhibitor.

claim: In vitro, the SPRTN-Y117C mutant protein has no detectable autocatalytic activity.
source: In vitro, the SPRTN-Y117C mutant protein has no detectable autocatalytic activity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A through in vitro cleavage assays.

claim: Recombinant SPRTN-∆C protein is catalytically active as it auto-cleaves into smaller cleavage fragments in in vitro reactions.
source: In sharp contrast to the SPRTN-Y117C, and to what is observed in cells upon SPRTN-∆C expression, recombinant SPRTN-∆C protein is catalytically active as it auto-cleaves into smaller cleavage fragments in in vitro reactions (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A through in vitro cleavage assays.

claim: Purified SPRTN cleaves itself and histone H3 in in vitro settings in a time-dependent manner.
source: To further characterize SPRTN as a protease, we showed that purified SPRTN cleaves itself and histone H3 in in vitro settings in a time-dependent manner (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B through in vitro cleavage assays.

claim: Histone H3 cleavage was not detected when treated with SPRTN-E112A.
source: Importantly, we did not detect histone H3 cleavage when treated with SPRTN-E112A.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B through in vitro cleavage assays.

claim: SPRTN-Y117C failed to cleave histone H3 at the latest time-point.
source: Similarly, SPRTN-Y117C also failed to cleave histone H3 at the latest time-point.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B through in vitro cleavage assays.

claim: SPRTN, but not SPRTN-E112A, can reduce the levels of full length Top2.
source: We found that SPRTN, but not SPRTN-E112A, can reduce the levels of full length Top2.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C through in vitro cleavage assays.

claim: The addition of recombinant ubiquitin can enhance not only Top2 cleavage, but also SPRTN self-cleavage.
source: Interestingly, the addition of recombinant ubiquitin can enhance not only Top2 cleavage, but also SPRTN self-cleavage, whereas addition of recombinant SUMO cannot mediate this enhanced effect (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C through in vitro cleavage assays.

claim: Addition of recombinant SUMO cannot enhance Top2 cleavage or SPRTN self-cleavage.
source: Interestingly, the addition of recombinant ubiquitin can enhance not only Top2 cleavage, but also SPRTN self-cleavage, whereas addition of recombinant SUMO cannot mediate this enhanced effect (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C through in vitro cleavage assays.

claim: The addition of DNA induces SPRTN self-cleavage in a time dependent manner, with enhanced SPRTN cleavage fragments seen at later time points.
source: The addition of DNA induces SPRTN self-cleavage in a time dependent manner, with enhanced SPRTN cleavage fragments seen at later time points.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A through time-course experiments.

claim: SPRTN self-cleavage is further enhanced when free ubiquitin is included in the reaction.
source: This effect is further enhanced when free ubiquitin is included in the reaction (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A through time-course experiments.

claim: The addition of ubiquitin has no effect on SPRTN-E112A or SPRTN-Y117C self-cleavage.
source: Importantly, the addition of ubiquitin has no effect on SPRTN-E112A or SPRTN-Y117C self-cleavage (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), ruling out the presence of a contaminating protease in our ubiquitin preparations.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and rules out contamination.

claim: SPRTN is a zinc-dependent metalloprotease that can proteolyze itself and other DNA binding proteins.
source: Taken together, these results clearly show that SPRTN is a zinc-dependent metalloprotease that can proteolyze itself and other DNA binding proteins, and that presence of free ubiquitin in the reaction enhances SPRTN cleavage activity.
evidence: This is concluded from the in vitro protease assays.

claim: Presence of free ubiquitin in the reaction enhances SPRTN cleavage activity.
source: Taken together, these results clearly show that SPRTN is a zinc-dependent metalloprotease that can proteolyze itself and other DNA binding proteins, and that presence of free ubiquitin in the reaction enhances SPRTN cleavage activity.
evidence: This is shown through in vitro assays with ubiquitin addition.

claim: SPRTN primary amino acid sequence contains at least three potential nuclear localization signals (NLS).
source: Careful analysis of the primary SPRTN amino acid sequence revealed the presence of at least three potential nuclear localization signals (NLS) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 through bioinformatic analysis.

claim: NLS3 lies between the PIP and UBZ domain and would clearly be missing in the SPRTN-∆C protein.
source: Of these three, one of them (NLS3) was a stronger NLS candidate for two reasons: (1) The NLS lies between the PIP and UBZ domain and would clearly be missing in the SPRTN-∆C protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the domain structure analysis.

claim: The NLS3 amino acid sequence is conserved across higher vertebrate SPRTN orthologues.
source: (2) The NLS amino acid sequence is conserved across higher vertebrate SPRTN orthologues (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A through sequence alignment.

claim: GFP-SPRTN expression is confined to the nucleus.
source: In agreement with previous reports, GFP-SPRTN expression is confined to the nucleus (Figure 5B) (Centore et al., 2012; Davis et al., 2012; Ghosal et al., 2012; Juhasz et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013; Lessel et al., 2014; Machida et al., 2012; Mosbech et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B through microscopy and supported by citations.

claim: The SPRTN-Y117C mutation has no effect on localization akin to catalytic inactive SPRTN-E112A mutant.
source: The SPRTN-Y117C mutation has no effect on localization akin to catalytic inactive SPRTN-E112A mutant.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B through microscopy.

claim: The GFP-SPRTN-∆C protein is evidently mislocalized to the cytoplasm.
source: However, the GFP-SPRTN-∆C protein is evidently mislocalized to the cytoplasm (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B through microscopy.

claim: SPRTN-∆C mislocalization suggests an obvious molecular explanation for compromised function in DPC removal.
source: This apparent SPRTN-∆C mislocalization suggests an obvious molecular explanation for compromised function in DPC removal.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization data.

claim: GFP-SPRTN-R408A L411A is mislocalized to the cytoplasm similarly to the GFP-SPRTN-∆C.
source: As expected, GFP-SPRTN-R408A L411A is mislocalized to the cytoplasm similarly to the GFP-SPRTN-∆C (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B through microscopy.

claim: The NLS fusion to GFP-SPRTN-∆C is sufficient for restoring nuclear expression.
source: The NLS fusion to GFP-SPRTN-∆C is sufficient for restoring nuclear expression (Figure 5B) and histone H3 cleavage in cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B through microscopy and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The addition of a heterologous NLS to SPRTN-∆C, as in SPRTN-∆C+NLS, enhances its Top2 resolvase activity relative to SPRTN-∆C.
source: As expected, the addition of a heterologous NLS to SPRTN-∆C, as in SPRTN-∆C+NLS, enhances its Top2 resolvase activity relative to SPRTN-∆C (Figure 5C and 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C through ICE assay.

claim: Removal of the NLS signal from full length SPRTN, as in SPRTN-R408A L411A, results in an attenuation of DPC resolvase activity.
source: It then follows, that removal of the NLS signal from full length SPRTN, as in SPRTN-R408A L411A, would result in an attenuation of DPC resolvase activity (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C through ICE assay.

claim: SPRTN-∆C is hypomorphic, at least in part, due to its mislocalized expression and its inability to bind to DNA.
source: Thus, we conclude that SPRTN-∆C is hypomorphic, at least in part, due to its mislocalized expression and its inability to bind to DNA.
evidence: This is concluded from the localization and DNA binding data.

claim: The NLS in SPRTN is both, necessary and sufficient, for proper nuclear localization and function.
source: In addition, we conclude that the NLS in SPRTN is both, necessary and sufficient, for proper nuclear localization and function.
evidence: This is concluded from the NLS mutation and rescue experiments.

claim: B-II-1 LCLs have more γ-H2AX staining in formaldehyde and Etoposide treatment compared to control LCLs.
source: Compared to control LCLs however, B-II-1 LCLs have more γ-H2AX staining in formaldehyde and Etoposide treatment as the majority of patient cells have increased DNA damage.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D through flow cytometry.

claim: B-II-1 LCLs contained modest increase in γ-H2AX staining when exposed to CPT treatment.
source: B-II-1 LCLs contained modest increase in γ-H2AX staining when exposed to CPT treatment.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D through flow cytometry.

claim: Top2cc are removed from DNA but with slower kinetics relative to control LCLs in B-II-1 patient cells.
source: Consistent with SPRTN-∆C and SPRTN-Y117C mutant variants being compromised for proteolytic activity, Top2cc are removed from DNA but with slower kinetics relative to control LCLs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E through ICE assay.

claim: SPRTN and Wss1 may form a common family of DPC resolving proteases in vivo.
source: SPRTN and Wss1 may form a common family of DPC resolving proteases in vivo (Stingele et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation and the functional similarities.

claim: SPRTN and Wss1 are functionally related as they are both implicated in the repair of DPCs.
source: Indeed, SPRTN and Wss1 are functionally related as they are both implicated in the repair of DPCs.
evidence: This is established from the experimental results in this study and previous work.

claim: The inability of SPRTN to complement Wss1 could be attributed, in part, to the differing ubiquitin and SUMO binding abilities that are also reflected in subsequent activation of their respective protease domains.
source: This inability of SPRTN to complement Wss1 could be attributed, in part, to the differing ubiquitin and SUMO binding abilities that are also reflected in subsequent activation of their respective protease domains.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the complementation results and binding differences.

claim: Wss1 is not essential in yeast, whereas SPRTN is essential in mammals.
source: In addition, Wss1 is not essential in yeast, whereas SPRTN is essential in mammals (Biggins et al., 2001; Maskey et al., 2014; Winzeler et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: wss1∆ yeast cells are resistant to CPT and mildly sensitive to formaldehyde, whereas SPRTN-KO MEFs are highly sensitive to CPT and formaldehyde.
source: The fact that wss1∆ yeast cells are resistant to CPT and mildly sensitive to formaldehyde, whereas SPRTN-KO MEFs are highly sensitive to CPT and formaldehyde strongly argues that partially overlapping pathways contribute to DPC bypass in yeast (Stingele et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation and the experimental results in this study.

claim: Partially overlapping pathways contribute to DPC bypass in yeast.
source: The fact that wss1∆ yeast cells are resistant to CPT and mildly sensitive to formaldehyde, whereas SPRTN-KO MEFs are highly sensitive to CPT and formaldehyde strongly argues that partially overlapping pathways contribute to DPC bypass in yeast (Stingele et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential sensitivities between yeast and mammalian cells.

claim: SPRTN is dispensable in C. elegans.
source: SPRTN is also dispensable in C. elegans (Mosbech et al., 2012), further underscoring the hypothesis that in lower eukaryotes such as in yeast and worms, other pathways can contribute to resolving DPCs.
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: In lower eukaryotes such as in yeast and worms, other pathways can contribute to resolving DPCs.
source: SPRTN is also dispensable in C. elegans (Mosbech et al., 2012), further underscoring the hypothesis that in lower eukaryotes such as in yeast and worms, other pathways can contribute to resolving DPCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the dispensability of SPRTN in lower eukaryotes.

claim: The activity of SPRTN must be carefully regulated to avoid indiscriminate proteolysis of DNA-associated proteins.
source: There are numerous proteins that are intimately associated with DNA, yet these proteins are spared from indiscriminate SPRTN-dependent proteolysis. Therefore, the activity of SPRTN must be carefully regulated.
evidence: This is logical inference from the observation that not all DNA-binding proteins are cleaved.

claim: Post-translational modification of SPRTN may dictate whether SPRTN can access proteins for proteolysis.
source: One potential explanation could be that post-translational modification of SPRTN dictates whether SPRTN can access proteins for proteolysis.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about regulation mechanisms.

claim: Mono-ubiquitylation of SPRTN may render it in a closed/inactive conformation.
source: Specifically, the mono-ubiquitylation of SPRTN may render it in a closed/inactive conformation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on analogy to Pol eta regulation.

claim: A mono-ubiquitin-mediated mechanism of inactivation exists for the translesion polymerase, Pol eta.
source: Indeed, we have previously uncovered a mono-ubiquitin-mediated mechanism of inactivation for the translesion polymerase, Pol eta (Bienko et al., 2010), setting precedent for this mode of regulation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Pol eta and SPRTN are both UBZ-containing proteins and both are mono-ubiquitylated in an UBZ-dependent manner.
source: Moreover, Pol eta and SPRTN are both UBZ-containing proteins and both are mono-ubiquitylated in an UBZ-dependent manner (Bienko et al., 2005; Centore et al., 2012; Mosbech et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mono-ubiquitylated SPRTN may be inactivated because its active site and/or DNA binding site is occluded akin to how Pol eta mono-ubiquitylation prevents its recruitment to PCNA.
source: It is conceivably possible that mono-ubiquitylated SPRTN is inactivated because its active site and/or DNA binding site is occluded akin to how Pol eta mono-ubiquitylation prevents its recruitment to PCNA.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on analogy to Pol eta.

claim: In trans binding to other ubiquitylated proteins in the vicinity may lead to allosteric activation resulting in the opening of the protease domain.
source: Alternatively, in trans binding to other ubiquitylated proteins in the vicinity may lead to allosteric activation resulting in the opening of the protease domain.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about activation mechanisms.

claim: The addition of ubiquitin, but not SUMO, promotes SPRTN cleavage of Top2 in vitro.
source: This model is supported by evidence that the addition of ubiquitin, but not SUMO, promotes SPRTN cleavage of Top2 in vitro.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C through in vitro assays.

claim: Binding to PCNA or p97 may contribute to step-wise activation of SPRTN in vivo.
source: Similarly, binding to PCNA or p97 may contribute to the same phenomena, leading to a step-wise activation process in vivo.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about activation mechanisms.

claim: SPRTN's proteolytic activity is restricted by a naturally occurring conformation that occludes the protease active site.
source: Based on these and other data we propose a model where SPRTN's proteolytic activity is restricted by a naturally occurring conformation that occludes the protease active site.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: Either substrate/DNA binding or de-ubiquitination of SPRTN leads to allosteric changes in SPRTN that expose its active site thus unleashing its proteolytic activity.
source: Either substrate/DNA binding or de-ubiquitination of SPRTN leads to allosteric changes in SPRTN that expose its active site thus unleashing its proteolytic activity.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: Binding to SUMO rather than to ubiquitin may act as a critical signal for Wss1 activation.
source: This mechanism appears different in the case of Wss1, whereby binding to SUMO rather than to ubiquitin may act as a critical signal for Wss1 activation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the differences between SPRTN and Wss1.
